This was the first HTB box I ever solved, very nice beginner boot2root that goes from IDOR to pcap analysis to binary privesc.

After connecting to the VPN, I began with doing an nmap scan on the IP. Three tcp ports open, one of them’s http. In my limited experience with these, you always start with the web service.

Going on the website takes you to a dashboard, some network event monitor service of sorts.

Poking around, I saw that the security snapshot section references snapshots based on their IDs. There’s nothing notable in my snapshot, but I wonder if I could access snapshot IDs outside of my own…

Turns out I can! And there’s a LOT more useful stuff in this, I presume. I found an IDOR!

Opening the pcap in wireshark, I found an unencrypted ftp login that exposes the password.

Connecting to the server’s FTP service, the same password works! Turns out the user flag can be directly accessed from here, a quick ls and I get the flag (bad pun I know).

Since the field said 32 char hex string, I assumed 6c96d019e266213b35e1681f2e089ba2 was my flag. Indeed it was! Very nice.

Now I knew the root flag had to be some sort of privesc through the SSH service.

First I tried to find any binaries that had SUID bits, but nothing notable. Then I tried looking for active processes in case there’s anything there, there wasn’t. I even tried to look for running services, but there was nothing really of note there either.

Then, after some googling on finding privesc binaries I learnt that getcap lets you find binaries with privileges that can be used for privesc. I didn’t know what python’s cap_setuid was, but it seemed like it could get me my flag.

Turns out my intuition was right, when python runs with cap_setuid, it has the privilege to spawn a shell with uid set to 0 (root) and through a neat oneliner I wrote I was able to spawn a root shell and cat the flag!

Yay, I solved my first HTB box!
